question: What remains when those on earth perish?

positions.position: God alone remains eternally, while every creature passes away.
positions.reasons: Muqatil compares 28:88; Tabari specifies jinn and humans; Abu Hayyan says every created thing is extinguished; Islahi links creation, provision, wisdom and sovereignty to its end and subsequent judgment; Ibn Ashur says mortality points to reckoning; Kuranyolu draws a call to live for God's pleasure.

positions.position: The universe is already perishing in its dependence, even while it appears to exist.
positions.reasons: Bursevi reports that dependent things lack self-subsisting existence; only the pre-eternal is real.

turns_on: Whether perishing is read as future death or as the present dependence of created existence.

question: What does 'the face of your Lord' denote here?

positions.position: God Himself, His enduring Essence or Reality.
positions.reasons: Muqatil cites 28:88. Nahhas compares 'face of the earth'; Tabarsi cites the face as the person's manifestation through proofs and Arabic idioms for the essence of an opinion or plan, including al-A'sha's poetry. Razi says seeing a face lets one know the whole person; Qurtubi cites Ibn Abbas, Ibn Furak and Abu al-Ma'ali; Biqai says the face, the noblest part, cannot endure apart from its possessor. Bursevi calls it a borrowing from the chief seat of the senses; Asad, Ibn Ashur and Islahi cite ordinary metonymy. Baydawi and Bursevi also describe the God-facing aspect of otherwise finite things. Elmalili says nominative dhu supports the Essence and excludes created relations.

positions.position: God as manifest through His signs and proofs.
positions.reasons: Wahidi's meaning scholars liken signs to a human face making a person apparent; Tabarsi combines this with reference to God Himself; Qurtubi reports it as an alternative.

positions.position: The Godward direction, aim, or aspect of beings, including the means of drawing near to Him.
positions.reasons: Tabrisi cites poetry joining God's face to deeds; Qurtubi reports the approach to God; Bursevi's Ibn al-Shaykh links direction with 'in God's side' (39:56), while Sa'di al-Mufti explains the aim as a genitive. Baydawi's Godward aspect is reported by Alusi and Elmalili; Shihab calls direction an alternative to essence. Tabatabai says this can encompass prophets, saints, religion, reward and nearness. Alusi objects that a deed reading does not fit universal perishing.

positions.position: Righteous deeds directed to God, or their enduring reward.
positions.reasons: Bursevi's Ibn al-Shaykh says only God-directed works escape passing; Elmalili says a deed is kept until its reward, which remains in its place. Alusi reports this but objects to its fit with universal perishing.

positions.position: A distinct divine attribute by which God turns toward those He honors.
positions.reasons: Qushayri reports it as an additional, unqualified attribute.

positions.position: God's noble attributes or sacred Name, which convey His blessings to creation.
positions.reasons: Tabatabai defines face as what a thing presents to or receives from another; creating, governing, mercy and provision reach creation through the attributes. The name finally designates the sacred Essence and remains unchanged by creatures' death.

positions.position: God's sustaining care for creatures, an attribute of His Essence.
positions.reasons: Elmalili reports some shaykhs' reading and says it too stresses essential permanence through lordship.

positions.position: The divine regard or bestowed existence through which contingent things exist.
positions.reasons: Alusi says God's attending and bestowing aspect remains while things perish continually; his metaphysical account makes face the relation to God, or existence bestowed on possible beings. Makdisi and Elmalili say possible beings otherwise lack existence.

positions.position: The special relation in which possible beings manifest divine presence.
positions.reasons: Alusi ascribes this to the theistic philosophers' metaphorical existence account; their possible beings mirror the self-subsistent Necessary, with reflections differing by relation.

positions.position: Divine affairs and manifestations of one Essence, apart from which created things have no independent being.
positions.reasons: Alusi distinguishes the realized Sufis' one-Essence account from philosophers' mirrors and says the two are often treated alike; see 6:91. Bursevi reads the abiding face as essential unity after relative plurality of Names passes.

turns_on: Whether face refers directly to God, an attribute or manifestation, or the Godward aspect and deeds of creation.

question: Can the divine 'face' be understood as a bodily organ?

positions.position: No; divine transcendence rules out a corporeal face.
positions.reasons: Razi argues from 28:88 that if face were an organ, other divine parts would perish; he says essence includes attributes, as a remaining garment includes color and size. Abu Hayyan excludes bodily limbs; Biqai invokes God's incomparability and freedom from need; Ibn Ashur says listeners know a head's bodily face is impossible.

positions.position: Affirm the revealed expression without asking how or assigning an interpretation, while denying likeness to creatures.
positions.reasons: Suyuti reports the majority of early Sunnis and hadith scholars, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan's jurist consensus, and al-Tirmidhi's imams; al-Juwayni reportedly returned to this early method. Elmalili and Ibn Ashur describe the same restraint; Ibn Ashur accepts it.

positions.position: Interpret attribute expressions figuratively in a manner fitting divine majesty.
positions.reasons: Suyuti reports a later Sunni method; Alusi identifies essence interpretation as later theologians' ta'wil; Ibn Ashur says successors and later scholars clarified it through rhetoric and regards that as sound.

turns_on: Whether to leave the nonbodily expression unprobed or explain its figurative meaning.

question: Do God's attributes remain with His Essence?

positions.position: Yes; the enduring Essence includes its attributes.
positions.reasons: Razi's garment analogy says the thing that remains retains color and dimensions; Qashani expressly includes all attributes; Ibn Ashur says the majesty-and-generosity qualification embraces transcendence, perfection, beauty and beneficence.

positions.position: Only the divine Essence remains; distinct attributes pass away.
positions.reasons: Study Quran reports the inference made by theologians separating Essence from Attributes, and reports Razi's objection that such a claim would require the wording 'nothing remains except the Face of thy Lord.'

turns_on: Whether the attributes belong with the Essence in what the verse calls enduring.

question: To whom does 'your Lord' address the verse?

positions.position: Every hearer is addressed.
positions.reasons: Razi says each person must attend to God alone; the singular prevents a pair of addressees from exempting each other. Bursevi extends it especially to humans and jinn; Ibn Ashur includes all hearers as the intended audience.

positions.position: The Prophet is the immediate addressee, to honor him.
positions.reasons: Razi allows this; Abu Hayyan and Alusi prefer it; Ibn Ashur says the ultimate audience nevertheless includes everyone who hears the Qur'an.

turns_on: Whether the singular address names the Prophet in particular or distributes the warning to each listener.

question: What does the word 'Lord' convey here?

positions.position: The one who nurtures and sustains.
positions.reasons: Razi reports rabb as a verbal noun for upbringing, by comparison with verbs of raising; alternatively it is an agent-like adjective from that noun. Biqai says God nurtures the Prophet by revelation toward unbounded knowledge.

question: Why say 'the face of your Lord' rather than simply 'your Lord' or another divine name?

positions.position: The wording asserts God's absolute permanence without implying that a subject remains under His lordship.
positions.reasons: Razi says Lord, Creator and Provider are agent names that could suggest continuing objects; even Allah may be explained as the worshipped one. Elmalili says face stresses the Essence's permanence as its attributes and lordship manifest.

positions.position: The face, as the noblest part, more eloquently conveys the whole enduring person.
positions.reasons: Biqai says a face cannot continue apart from its possessor and its mention is more eloquent than mentioning the possessor directly.

positions.position: The wording evokes care, gentleness and the sūrah's blessings.
positions.reasons: Razi contrasts the gentleness of direct address to the Lord with the might of abiding; Study Quran reports that 'your Lord' suits the recurring blessing and bounty theme.

positions.position: This passage's lordly sustaining favors suit 'your Lord'; other passages use 'face of Allah' for worship or charity.
positions.reasons: Razi compares 2:115 and 30:38. Ibn Ashur likewise notes direction and charitable intention in 2:115 and 76:9.

turns_on: Which force of the chosen expression the commentator emphasizes.

question: How is 'rabb' ordinarily constructed in Arabic?

positions.position: It is ordinarily annexed; when unannexed it is accompanied by another description.

question: Is 'rabb' originally a verbal noun or a derived description?

positions.position: It may be a verbal noun meaning upbringing.
positions.reasons: Razi compares verbs meaning to raise or nurture.

positions.position: It may be a derived adjective meaning one who nurtures.
positions.reasons: Razi compares agent names and qualities formed from verbal nouns.

turns_on: Its proposed morphological origin.

question: How is ذُو read, and what does it modify?

positions.position: The common nominative ذُو modifies وَجْهُ.
positions.reasons: Tabari, Nahhas, Wahidi, Jishumi, Abu Hayyan, Samin, Nasafi, Elmalili and Study Quran attach the adjective to face; Wahidi says a Lord adjunct would require ذِي. Ibn al-Jazari says every codex agrees on wāw here, so it cannot be an insertion. Alusi connects this to God's uninjured self-sufficiency and future generosity.

positions.position: The reported genitive ذِي modifies رَبِّكَ.
positions.reasons: Attributed to Abdullah/Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy by Tabari, Nahhas, Jishumi, Abu Hayyan, Samin and Alusi; it makes the Lord the grammatical bearer of the epithet. Ibn al-Jazari distinguishes the canonical text's unanimous wāw.

positions.position: The nominative may be detached for praise, with an implied 'He is'; it then describes the Lord.
positions.reasons: Tabatabai proposes an elided predicate; Alusi says this parse is used particularly if face means action or direction.

turns_on: The case ending and whether the epithet follows face, Lord, or an implied predicate.

question: What further recitational variants affect the epithet?

positions.position: At the sūrah's ending the seven readers differ in the corresponding phrase.
positions.reasons: Al-Samin notes the contrast with this occurrence.

positions.position: Reports differ on Ibn Dhakwan's imāla in الإكرام.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jazari says al-Tajrid records only imāla through al-Akhfash and several transmitters, alongside عمران (3:36) and إكراههن (24:33).

turns_on: Which occurrence or pronunciation the report concerns.

question: What does 'majesty' mean here?

positions.position: Divine greatness, exaltation, sovereignty and deservingness of praise.
positions.reasons: Wahidi and Qurtubi derive jalal from jalla, to be great; Tabarsi adds supreme beneficence as the source of favors; Ibn Abbas is reported in Ibn Kathir and Durr as glossing it greatness and pride. Qashani describes veils and overpowering dominion; Elmalili speaks of greatness that overwhelms all.

positions.position: Absolute independence and freedom from every need or unworthy quality.
positions.reasons: Baydawi joins self-sufficiency with bounty; Bursevi and Alusi report the same; Biqai says it excludes what is unworthy of God.

positions.position: God's awe-inspiring transcendence, which monotheists affirm.
positions.reasons: Abu Hayyan lists transcendence above likeness to creation and awe before God; Alusi distinguishes intrinsic perfection beyond comprehension from felt awe.

turns_on: Whether majesty is glossed chiefly as greatness, independence, or awe-inspiring transcendence.

question: Is 'jalāl' used only of God?

positions.position: Only God deserves or is described by jalāl.
positions.reasons: Wahidi reports al-Asma'i's usage rule; Abu Ali allows that al-Asma'i may mean exclusive deservingness after Islam. Raghib says the full title uniquely belongs to God.

positions.position: Arabic poetry also applies jalāl to someone other than God.
positions.reasons: Wahidi's Abu Ali cites a poem, possibly pre-Islamic, qualifying al-Asma'i's claim.

turns_on: Whether the claim concerns all historical usage or the proper divine title.

question: What does 'honor' or 'generosity' mean here?

positions.position: God honors and benefits His servants through grace, pardon and bounty.
positions.reasons: Wahidi specifies prophets through grace and, through Hasan and al-Kalbi, adherents of God's religion through forgiveness; Baghawi and Tabarsi name prophets and friends; Ibn Jawzi says God raises devotees' ranks; Nasafi says pardon and beneficence. Biqai makes it divine action, and Elmalili extends care even to the perishing.

positions.position: Servants must honor God through worship, praise, reverence and avoiding disbelief or shirk.
positions.reasons: Wahidi mentions worship and praise for favors; al-Khattabi calls both terms verbal nouns deserving human reverence and honor, without denial; Qurtubi requires declaring God free of partners; Ibn Kathir says to revere and obey without defiance. Ibn Jawzi compares the distribution of God and servant actions in 74:56.

positions.position: God's incomparable honor: none is more honorable or greater.
positions.reasons: Wahidi reports Ibn Abbas's gloss.

positions.position: God grants nearness through manifestations of gentleness and mercy.
positions.reasons: Qashani connects generosity to attributes appearing and the Essence manifesting in mercy.

turns_on: Whether ikram names God's gifts, the servant's duty to honor Him, or God's own supreme honor.

question: What does the combined title 'Possessor of Majesty and Honor' express?

positions.position: It joins God's transcendent greatness with generous beneficence.
positions.reasons: Baydawi calls these absolute self-sufficiency and general bounty; Bursevi and Alusi pair independence with complete favor; Ibn Ashur says the pair covers transcendence, perfection, beauty and service to creatures; Study Quran relates the pair to Majesty and Beauty.

positions.position: The title can mark God's worthiness of reverence and His honoring of servants respectively.
positions.reasons: Ibn Jawzi allows one noun to name a divine attribute and the other a servant's act, comparing 74:56; Abu Hayyan reports God as the giver of majesty and honor to sincere servants.

positions.position: Majesty denotes negated limitations; generosity or beauty denotes affirmed perfections.
positions.reasons: Alusi reports al-Kirmani's examples of no partner versus life and knowledge, but says the division needs examination. Study Quran reports a Shiite scheme of Beauty's inherent positive attributes and Majesty's denial of bodily limits.

positions.position: The name ultimately denotes the sacred Essence.
positions.reasons: Tabatabai says the paired names of majesty and beauty name God Himself, comparing 55:78.

positions.position: It is among God's uniquely exalted names.
positions.reasons: Alusi and Elmalili report Raghib's description of the full title as unique to God and one of His greatest descriptions.

turns_on: How the two qualities divide between transcendence, positive perfection, God's action, and human response.

question: What is reported about invoking God by this title?

positions.position: The Prophet urges persistent repetition of 'O Possessor of Majesty and Honor' in supplication.
positions.reasons: Qurtubi transmits Anas and an Ibn Mas'ud attribution; Abu Ubayd explains ilzaz as adhering and insistent prayer. Nasafi, Bursevi, Alusi and Elmalili report the same exhortation, with Alusi and Elmalili also naming Rabi'a ibn Amir.

positions.position: The Prophet told a man who invoked this name that his prayer had been answered.
positions.reasons: Nasafi and Bursevi transmit the incident; Bursevi draws the prospect of acceptance.

positions.position: A man invoking this name heard that his request had been heard.
positions.reasons: Qurtubi transmits Sa'id al-Maqburi's report.

positions.position: Invocation including the title is a supplication by God's Greatest Name, which draws an answer.
positions.reasons: Alusi reports Anas's account of a man; Elmalili specifies praise, generosity, majesty, life and self-subsistence in the prayer.

positions.position: A transmitted supplication joins this title to God's living, sustaining and creating power.
positions.reasons: Ibn Kathir cites the request for mercy, rectitude and protection from dependence on self or creation.

positions.position: A man prayed by God's generous face; another wording called it the abiding beautiful face.
positions.reasons: Durr reports the man and al-Bayhaqi's variant wording.

turns_on: The reports concern distinct exhortations, answered prayers and transmitted formulas.

question: How does the verse relate to the death of creatures?

positions.position: The verse states a universal end and anticipates reckoning and reward.
positions.reasons: Ibn Kathir reports Qatada that God tells of creation and then its passing; Ibn Ashur says the reminder of death looks ahead to recompense; Islahi says none can challenge God's judgment or intercede without leave.

positions.position: Death is a favor because it leads from earthly trial to recompense.
positions.reasons: Tabrisi says death equalizes creatures and warns of life's end; immediate reward would compel action and deprive it of merit. Tabatabai calls worldly life a preparation for the afterlife; Kuranyolu points to lasting happiness through a life pleasing God.

turns_on: Whether the point is the coming end and judgment or why that end counts as a favor.

question: What did the angels conclude when the verse was revealed?

positions.position: They first inferred the earthly beings had perished, then learned their own mortality from 28:88.
positions.reasons: Muqatil says they wondered how life could benefit people and were reassured that all die; Wahidi attributes the report to al-Kalbi and Muqatil.

positions.position: They first thought Adam's children had perished, then learned their own mortality from 'every soul tastes death' (3:185).
positions.reasons: Bursevi adds that angels' subtle bodies and attached spirits perish but lofty immaterial spirits do not.

turns_on: The report differs on the later verse and on what exactly perishes.

question: Where should a reciter pause across verses 26–27?

positions.position: Continue past 'all on earth perish' until God's abiding face has been recited.
positions.reasons: Wahidi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jazari, Durr and Suyuti transmit al-Sha'bi's direction; Suyuti cites Ibn Abi Hatim. Burhan says the two statements do not conflict.

question: How does this verse connect to other Qur'anic passages?

positions.position: It parallels 28:88: all things perish except God's face.
positions.reasons: Muqatil, Razi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir, Elmalili, Asad and Study Quran invoke the parallel; Ibn Kathir also connects seeking the face to 18:28 and 76:9.

positions.position: The closing title in 55:78 echoes 55:27 and confirms God's exclusive exaltation.
positions.reasons: Islahi says no partner shares majesty and bounty; Study Quran says the echo places God beyond earthly and heavenly blessings; Tabatabai also compares 55:78.

turns_on: Which passage supplies the comparison: 28:88 or the sūrah's own ending.

question: What role does this verse play in the sūrah's movement?

positions.position: It closes the worldly blessings and turns toward the Hereafter.
positions.reasons: Study Quran locates the turn after vv. 10–25; Abu Hayyan contrasts the passing world and enduring face with the sūrah's later lasting Paradise and blessed name; Bursevi says generosity after death includes resurrection and eternal bliss.

positions.position: It sets God's permanence against creation's transient dualities and grounds the repeated favor refrain.
positions.reasons: Study Quran contrasts God with what passes; Ibn Ashur says the ensuing question about favors follows because His great and generous treatment never ceases; Islahi traces the passage to the earth since verse 10.

turns_on: Which structural connection within the sūrah is emphasized.

question: What rhetorical effect joins human death to divine permanence?

positions.position: The sequence blends consolation of creatures and praise of God's enduring majesty and generosity.
positions.reasons: Suyuti calls the ten-word turn iftinan, combining two modes, consolation and praise.

positions.position: The verse names a part, 'face,' for the whole divine Self.
positions.reasons: Suyuti compares body-wide states expressed through faces and hands and actions of prayer naming whole prayer, citing 2:144, 88:8, 88:3, 2:286, 2:184, 17:78, 76:26, 2:43 and 5:95.

positions.position: God's majesty and generosity signal that kindness continues beyond creatures' deaths.
positions.reasons: Bursevi says resurrection to lasting bliss is the greatest blessing.

turns_on: The notes identify distinct rhetorical effects of the same juxtaposition.

question: What inward insight does the enduring face convey?

positions.position: Divine disclosure and veiling govern what creatures can witness.
positions.reasons: Sulami's al-Wasiti says God inwardly discloses in this life while veiling by wonders; in the next He gives outwardly but shields creatures according to their capacity.

positions.position: The knower witnesses God's abiding presence through creation.
positions.reasons: Elmalili reports realized knowers who see nothing apart from God; Ibn Ata calls creation darkness lit only by divine manifestation and says overlooking God in, before, after or alongside it veils knowledge.

positions.position: Majesty and generosity manifest as overpowering veils and merciful nearness.
positions.reasons: Qashani describes luminous and dark veils, dominion, attributes, gentleness and mercy.

turns_on: Whether the inward lesson concerns veiling, witnessing, or the paired manifestations.

question: Does 'face' derive from confrontation?

positions.position: No; the organ name preceded terms for facing or confrontation.
positions.reasons: Razi rejects the reverse derivation found in some legal books and treats later related forms as transferred from the earlier organ word.

positions.position: The original sense may be direction, with essence a later allusion.
positions.reasons: Alusi reports this alternative origin account.

turns_on: Which sense is taken as the lexical starting point.

question: How does the title's majesty-and-generosity description identify the face?

positions.position: The title identifies God's Essence, which bears these attributes.
positions.reasons: Ibn Ashur says the epithet embraces transcendence, perfection and beneficence; Elmalili argues that created God-facing relations cannot bear it, so face means Essence.

positions.position: The title can describe a noble divine Name or attribute and thereby ultimately the Essence.
positions.reasons: Tabatabai says applying the name to the name ultimately names God; creation's passing leaves the name unchanged.

turns_on: Whether the modifier attaches semantically to the Essence directly or to a divine name or attribute.

question: How do different accounts of existence frame this verse?

positions.position: Possible beings have actual existence inhering in them.
positions.reasons: Alusi identifies this as the view of most philosophers and theologians, in contrast with metaphorical-existence accounts.

positions.position: Created existence is metaphorical, explained either as divine manifestation or as affairs of one Essence.
positions.reasons: Alusi distinguishes the theistic philosophers' mirror model from realized Sufis' one-Essence model; his note says the two are often assimilated.

turns_on: Whether possible beings possess actual existence or are described as existent through divine manifestation.

question: How is this verse's 'face' compared with other divine attribute expressions?

positions.position: It serves as a comparison for treating an apparent body-part term as emphatic.
positions.reasons: Suyuti reports Mujahid's comparison of the 'hand' in 38:75 with 'the Face of your Lord' here; al-Baghawi rejects the hand-as-addition reading because it would erase Adam's distinction from Satan.
